commentaries.index_excerpt: Eight classical commentaries on the Qur’an, translated in full on the verses that tell the story of Jesus: his birth, his signs, the cross and his raising.
index_intro: The Qur’an speaks of Jesus, son of Mary, in some 90 verses, and for 13 centuries Muslim commentators have written on each of them: what the words mean, what the Prophet and his Companions said about them, and what happened at the manger, in the temple, at the table and at the cross. Those commentaries are the Islamic record of the life of Jesus, and most of them have never been put into English. This part of the website gives them in full, verse by verse, for the passages that tell his story: his family and birth, his signs and his disciples, the plot against him, the cross and his raising, and the questioning on the Last Day.

The translations cover 8 works, from the tenth century to the twentieth, and they are complete: every opinion a commentator records is here, with the chain of transmission he gives for it, every verse of poetry he cites for a word’s meaning, and every grammatical argument he makes, because the reader who wants to know what Islam has said of Jesus should have the whole of it. The same texts are woven, passage by passage, into The Gospel According to Islam, so that the gospel and its commentary are read together.

index_after: Each commentary is given on its own page for each passage, in the order of the verses, under a heading for the verse or verses it treats. Qur’anic quotations within the commentary are in bold, with the reference where it can be identified. Where a commentator records several opinions, they are listed; where he cites a line of poetry for a word, it is set as a quotation; where he gives a chain of transmission, it is given in full, with “related to us” for ḥaddathanā and “from” for ʿan. The translator’s notes are numbered and identify names, places, terms and variant readings; they never summarise or replace the text.
The classical commentators quote one another freely, so the reader will meet the same report more than once, sometimes with a different chain, and the repetition shows how the report travelled.

The reports in these commentaries are of 2 kinds, and the commentators themselves say so. Some go back to the Prophet and are weighed by the rules of ḥadīth. Many more are what the early Muslims heard from converts from Judaism and Christianity, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār and Wahb ibn Munabbih above all, and are called isrāʾīliyyāt; Ibn Kathīr in particular marks them and warns against building doctrine on them. They are kept here because they are part of the record, and because several of them preserve Christian traditions, about the Last Supper, the arrest and the substitution at the cross, that are older than any Muslim book.
## On the sources and the translation

The Arabic texts are the standard printed editions as published without restriction at tafsir.app, and, for Tanwīr al-Miqbās, at the Shamela library (shamela.ws, book 12877); all 8 works are in the public domain. The English renderings were prepared for this website and are released with it; they have not been checked by a second translator, and the Arabic source of every passage is named so that it can be compared. The editors’ modern apparatus, their footnotes on manuscripts and chains, is not part of the classical text and is not translated. Corrections are welcome through the contact page and are recorded in the corrections log.

Tafsīr is the Muslim discipline of explaining the Qur’an: the meaning of its words, the occasions on which its verses were revealed, the reports of the Prophet and his Companions about them, and the rulings and lessons drawn from them. The great commentaries run to many volumes; the pages here give what 8 of them say on the verses about Jesus.
? Why translate the whole commentary and not the parts about Jesus?

Because a selection is itself an argument, and this website wants the reader to see the record. Every page carries all that the commentator wrote on the verse, including the grammar, the poetry and the chains of transmission, so that what he said about Jesus is read in the place and the company he gave it.
? Do the commentators agree that Jesus was not crucified?

Yes. From al-Ṭabarī in the tenth century to al-Saʿdī in the twentieth, every commentary translated here reads 4:157 as the Qur’an states it: the Jews did not kill him and did not crucify him, but another was made to resemble him and God raised Jesus to Himself. They differ about who the other man was, whether a disciple who volunteered or the man sent to seize him, and about whether Jesus tasted death for some hours before he was raised. None of them says he died on the cross.
? Are these the “Israelite tales” Muslims are warned about?

Some of the reports are. The commentators mark the stories that came through Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Wahb ibn Munabbih and the People of the Book, and Ibn Kathīr in particular says they may be related but not relied on. They are translated here because they are part of what was said, and because they preserve early Christian traditions in Arabic.
? Which translation of the Qur’an do the commentaries quote?

None. The Qur’anic phrases within the commentaries are translated afresh with the commentary, since the commentator is often explaining the very word a translation would have to choose, and the reference is given so that the verse can be read in the site’s translation on the Qur’anic passages.
? Why are there no Shia commentaries?

The 8 works here are the ones most read across the Sunni world and the ones the site owner asked for. The Shia commentaries, al-Ṭūsī’s al-Tibyān and al-Ṭabrisī’s Majmaʿ al-bayān above all, read these verses in the same way on the birth, the signs and the raising of Jesus, and may be added.

quran_passages.title: The Qur’an on Jesus
quran_passages.excerpt: Every passage of the Qur’an on Jesus and his teachings, with headings and notes.
intro: Every passage of the Qur’an on Jesus and his teachings, as Alham Ahmed gathered them in The Gospel According to the Quran: Jesus and His Teachings (Toronto: Noor Lal Foundation, 2021), with the compilation’s headings and notes. Each verse is numbered by chapter and verse. Many of them are set among the sections of The Gospel According to Islam.
source: The passages, their headings and their notes are from Alham Ahmed, The Gospel According to the Quran: Jesus and His Teachings, first edition (Toronto: Noor Lal Foundation, 2021), © 2021 Alham Ahmed. The translation of the Qur’an in that compilation is The Clear Quran by Dr. Mustafa Khattab, which the compiler uses with the permission of the Al-Furqaan Foundation (theclearquran.org). The compilation closes with God’s Beautiful Names (59:22-24) after Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ; this page gives every passage in the order of the Qur’an. Every source of the website is listed on the credits page.
